### Task 1 Slate Health Check


```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)
library(broom)
library(brms)
library(broom.mixed)
library(rstanarm)


movies <- read.csv("data/movies.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

genre_focus <- c(
  "Action",
  "Comedy",
  "Drama",
  "Horror",
  "Animation"
)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = revenue / budget,
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )

focus_genre_movies <- movies_clean |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% genre_focus)

```

Data Cleaning

Before any analysis was conducted, missing-data placeholders were identified and replaced with NA rather than removed. Per the variable dictionary, budget values of exactly $0 or below $10,000 are placeholder entries, and revenue values of $0 indicate missing box-office data. Rather than dropping these rows entirely, the affected values were converted to NA, retaining all 3,426 films in the five focus genres. Rows with NA budget or revenue are excluded automatically by R when calculating financial summaries and plots, but are retained for analyses such as franchise composition that do not require financial data.

###   Summary tables

```{r}
#| output: true
# Budget
movies_clean |>
  summarise(
    n      = sum(!is.na(budget_m)),
    mean   = round(mean(budget_m,            na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    median = round(median(budget_m,          na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    sd     = round(sd(budget_m,              na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Q1     = round(quantile(budget_m, 0.25,  na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Q3     = round(quantile(budget_m, 0.75,  na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    max    = round(max(budget_m,             na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary Statistics for Movie Budgets"
  )

# ROI
movies_clean |>
  summarise(
    n      = sum(!is.na(roi)),
    mean   = round(mean(roi,            na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median = round(median(roi,          na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd     = round(sd(roi,              na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q1     = round(quantile(roi, 0.25,  na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q3     = round(quantile(roi, 0.75,  na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    max    = round(max(roi,             na.rm = TRUE), 0)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary Statistics for Return on Investment (ROI)"
  )
```

The typical film cost \$25M to produce (median budget) and returned 2.3x its budget at the box office (median ROI). The mean ROI of 13.6x is not a reliable benchmark — it is driven almost entirely by a handful of micro-budget Horror films with extreme returns, most notably Paranormal Activity (\~12,890x ROI). Franchise films represent just 7% of the historical slate, with Originals making up the remaining 93%.

**Note: To make visualisation clear, the genres are divided into categories, with a standard of more and less than 250 movies per genre for further analysis.**


## Overall Production Budget Distribution

@fig-overall shows a positively skewed distribution of production budgets.This suggests that high production budgets are relatively uncommon, while most films are produced with more modest budgets. The Head of Production should consider this skewed distribution when planning future budgets, as a small number of high-budget films may influence the overall mean.

```{r}
#| label: fig-overall
#| fig-cap: "Overall production budget distribution across all genres."
#| output: true

# Overall budget distribution

budget_plot_data <- movies_clean |>
  filter(
    !is.na(budget),
    budget > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(budget_m = budget / 1e6)

# Plot overall budget distribution
ggplot(budget_plot_data, aes(x = budget_m)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "steelblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Overall Production Budget Distribution",
    x = "Production Budget ($ millions)",
    y = "Number of Movies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()



```

## Slate Trends Over Time (2000–2016) 

Franchise films make up 7% of the overall slate. Horror (21%) and Action (11%) have the highest franchise concentration; Drama sits lowest at just 1%.


```{r}
trend_summary <- movies_clean |>
  filter(release_year >= 2000, release_year <= 2016) |>
  group_by(release_year) |>
  summarise(
    n_films       = n(),
    median_budget = median(budget_m,  na.rm = TRUE),
    median_roi    = median(roi,        na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_franchise = sum(franchise_status == "Franchise") / n() * 100,
    .groups       = "drop"
  )
```


Franchise share increased towards 2016, reaching approximately 16%. Median production budgets generally declined from around $33 million in 2000 to $22 million in 2014–2015, before recovering slightly. In contrast, median ROI increased after 2010, reaching approximately 2.9 in 2016.

```{r}
#| output: true

trend_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(median_budget, median_roi, pct_franchise),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,
    median_budget  = "Median Budget (USD millions)",
    median_roi     = "Median ROI",
    pct_franchise  = "Franchise Share (%)"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = release_year, y = value)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#5B8DB8", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "#5B8DB8", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
              colour = "#C9485B", linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Slate Trends Over Time (2000–2016)",
    subtitle = "Red dashed = LOESS trend",
    x        = "Release Year",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2016, 4))
```


The Head of Production should consider these differences when evaluating opportunities to develop new original projects or invest in franchise films. However, the percentages describe the composition of the slate rather than financial success, so they should be considered alongside budget and ROI results before making investment decisions.


## Summary for the Head of Production

The overall budget distribution is positively skewed, with most films having lower budgets. Action and Adventure show wider budget ranges. Originals account for 94.6% of films, while franchises represent 5.4%. Horror has the highest franchise share among genres with over 250 films (15.7%), while Science Fiction leads among lower-volume genres (14.6%).

ROI varies across genres, with some films earning well above their production budgets. From 2000 to 2016, median ROI generally increased after 2010, reaching approximately 2.9 in 2016. Median budgets declined before recovering slightly, while franchise share rose to around 16%.

Zero budgets and revenues were treated as missing, and blank text values were converted to NA. Records with invalid budgets or missing genres were excluded from relevant plots, but the original dataset was retained. These limitations should be considered when using budget, ROI, genre and franchise trends to guide production decisions.




# Task 2

```{r}
t2 <- movies |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = revenue / budget,
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )
```

Budgets below \$10,000 are placeholders, so they were set to `NA` and no rows were deleted. Films with no usable budget are left out of the budget comparison only, because a median cannot be calculated without a budget. @tbl-t2-missing shows how many films this affects.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-missing
#| tbl-cap: "Films with and without a usable budget, by franchise status"
#| output: true
movies |>
  filter(!is.na(franchise_status)) |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(
    films = n(),
    usable_budget = sum(!is.na(budget)),
    missing_budget = sum(is.na(budget)),
    pct_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(budget)), 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Franchise status", "Films", "Usable budget", "Missing budget", "% missing"))
```


### 1. Comparing the budget distributions


```{r}

#| label: fig-t2plot
#| fig-cap: "Budget distributions by franchise status (log scale, axis labelled in dollars)"
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8
#| output: true


ggplot(t2, aes(x = budget, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8),
    labels = c("$0.1M", "$1M", "$10M", "$100M")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Franchise budgets sit higher, but the two groups overlap heavily",
    x = "Production budget (log scale)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Franchise status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

Franchise films generally have higher production budgets than original films, although the distributions overlap considerably. Original films are more concentrated at lower budgets, while franchises tend towards higher spending.


```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-box
#| fig-cap: "Budget by franchise status (log scale). The line in each box is the median."
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 8
#| output: true
ggplot(t2, aes(x = budget, y = franchise_status)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8),
    labels = c("$0.1M", "$1M", "$10M", "$100M")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Production budget (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-t2-box confirms that franchise films have a higher median budget than original films. However, both groups show substantial variation, indicating that franchise status alone does not determine production spending.

### 2. Interval estimate for the difference in median budget

We used a 95% percentile bootstrap interval: each group was resampled with replacement at its own size, Franchise median minus Original median was calculated, this was repeated 5,000 times, and the middle 95% was taken. All calculations are in dollars.

```{r}
#| label: t2-boot

obs_diff <- t2 |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(
    median_budget = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    diff = median_budget[franchise_status == "Franchise"] -
           median_budget[franchise_status == "Original"]
  ) |>
  pull(diff)

perform_bootstrap <- function(bootstrap_number) {
  t2 |>
    group_by(franchise_status) |>
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) |>
    summarise(
      median_budget = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    summarise(
      boot_diff = median_budget[franchise_status == "Franchise"] -
                  median_budget[franchise_status == "Original"]
    ) |>
    mutate(bootstrap_sample = bootstrap_number)
}

bootstrap_results <- map_dfr(1:5000, perform_bootstrap)

ci <- quantile(
  bootstrap_results$boot_diff,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975),
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Difference in median budget (Franchise minus Original) with 95% bootstrap interval (USD millions)"
#| output: true


tibble(observed = obs_diff, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2]) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ round(.x / 1e6, 1))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Observed difference", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-boot
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the difference in median budget. Solid line: observed difference. Dashed lines: 95% interval."
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 7
#| output: true

bootstrap_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = boot_diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = ~ paste0("$", .x / 1e6, "M")) +
  labs(x = "Franchise median minus Original median", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The observed difference in median budget is \$`r round(obs_diff / 1e6, 1)`M, and the 95% interval runs from \$`r round(ci[1] / 1e6, 1)`M to \$`r round(ci[2] / 1e6, 1)`M (@tbl-t2-ci, @fig-t2-boot). The interval does not include zero, so the typical Franchise budget is higher than the typical Original budget.

### 3. Does this support leadership's concern?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-concern
#| tbl-cap: "Share of films and budget, and proportion of low and high budgets, by franchise status"
#| output: true
t2 |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(
    n_films = n(),
    share_of_films = n() / nrow(t2),
    share_of_budget = sum(budget) / sum(t2$budget),
    under_10M = mean(budget < 10e6),
    over_100M = mean(budget > 100e6)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(share_of_films:over_100M, ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Franchise status", "Films", "Share of films", "Share of budget",
                             "Under $10M", "Over $100M"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-revenue
#| tbl-cap: "Share of total revenue by franchise status (films with revenue recorded)"
#| output: true

movies |>
  filter(!is.na(revenue), !is.na(franchise_status)) |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(total_revenue = sum(revenue)) |>
  mutate(share_of_revenue = round(total_revenue / sum(total_revenue), 3)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Franchise status", "Total revenue", "Share of revenue"))
```

Leadership's concern is only partly supported. Franchise films do indeed have larger budget per movie, where 22% of them have a budget higher than \$100M whereas only 6.5% of Originals do that (@tbl-t2-concern). However, Originals are not primarily small movies because 27% of them have budgets less than \$10M. 

Franchise films represent 6% of films, have 10% of budget (@tbl-t2-concern) and 14% of revenue (@tbl-t2-revenue), so Originals provide most of both expenses and income. It is an observation, so it only reveals budget gap without providing evidence on causation. Moreover, 23% of Originals do not have their budget specified at all compared to 10% of Franchise films (@tbl-t2-missing), so the actual gap may be even larger.

### 4. Investment advice

The data doesn't indicate that Originals are constrained by smaller budgets. This is the optimal approach: keep a few high-budget Franchise movies and increase the number of mid-budget Originals instead of considering Originals as small investments. The only problem to look out for is the extremely high Franchise budgets, because a couple of movies can affect the whole slate negatively. It doesn't say anything about return on investment, and so the optimal mix will include the results from Tasks 3 and 4.

### Summary for the Head of Production

We compared Franchise and Original budgets using the median, which is not affected by some very costly movies. An average Franchise movie had an estimated budget of \$40M while an average Original had an estimated budget of \$22M. With 95% confidence we estimate that the real difference lies in the interval from \$9M to \$26M.. Franchise movies have higher budget on average but there is significant overlap between the two distributions, Original movies are not mostly low-budget movies, and Franchise movies represent only 10% of the total budget. We recommend maintaining some Franchise movies and developing mid-budget Originals.

# Task 3 

## Part A

Universal Pictures was selected as Meridian Pictures’ benchmark. After filtering invalid budgets, 260 films remained. The mean budget was $41.57 million, the median was $30.50 million, and the standard deviation was $37.89 million. The higher mean indicates right-skewness, while the large standard deviation shows substantial budget variation. Therefore, a probability distribution is more useful than a single average for modelling production costs.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#| include: false

# Fitting in the data with normal distribution

Universal_budget <- movies |>
  dplyr::filter(primary_company == "Universal Pictures") |>
  dplyr::select(title, id, status, primary_genre, budget) |>
  dplyr::mutate(budget = as.double(budget))

#checking for any negative, zero or other anomaly in budget

Universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    total_films = n(),
    missing_budgets = sum(is.na(budget)),
    zero_budgets = sum(budget == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    negative_budgets = sum(budget < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    positive_budgets = sum(budget > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


#Summary statistics

budget_summary <- Universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_budget = mean(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_budget = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_budget = sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#creating the table out of the summary statistics

budget_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budget Summary",
    subtitle = "Descriptive statistics of historical film budgets"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    n = "Number of Films",
    mean_budget = "Mean Budget (USD)",
    median_budget = "Median Budget (USD)",
    sd_budget = "Standard Deviation (USD)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_budget, median_budget, sd_budget),
    decimals = 2,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = n,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Historical Universal Pictures film budget data."
)

```

### Assessment of the Normal Distribution

Universal Pictures’ production budgets are positively skewed, with most films having lower budgets and a few requiring much higher investment. The fitted normal curve does not capture this asymmetry, suggesting that a right-skewed distribution may better represent production budgets and their associated probabilities.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#plotting the graph 

ggplot(Universal_budget, aes(x = budget)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(
      mean = mean(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm= TRUE),
      sd= sd(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm= TRUE)
      
    ),
    colour = "brown",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    colour = "darkblue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budgets",
    subtitle = "Histogram with fitted normal distribution",
    x = "Production Budget (USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Choice of the alternative distribution and modelling

To identify a realistic probability model, normal, log-normal, Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions were considered. Their fitted curves and Q-Q plots were used to assess how closely the theoretical distributions represented the observed budgets, while AIC was used to compare their relative fit. The final model will be selected based on the AIC results and supporting diagnostic plots.

**Note :Budgets were then divided by 10,000,000 to improve numerical convenience during model estimation while preserving their relative distribution.**

```{r}
Universal_budget_clean <- Universal_budget |>
  filter(
    !is.na(budget),
    is.finite(budget),
    budget > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(budget_millions = budget / 10000000)

budget_values <- Universal_budget_clean$budget_millions


gamma_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "gamma"
)

weibull_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "weibull"
)

exponential_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "exponential"
)

```

## Graphical Representation of Model Choice

@fig-budget-distributions compares the Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions fitted to Universal Pictures' production budgets. The observed budgets are positively skewed, with most films concentrated at lower budget levels and a smaller number of films having substantially higher budgets.

```{r}
#| label: fig-budget-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of fitted Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions for Universal Pictures' production budgets."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#plotting the three fits in histogram

make_plot <- function(curve, distribution_name, curve_colour) {

  ggplot(
    data.frame(budget_values = budget_values),
    aes(x = budget_values)
  ) +

    geom_histogram(
      aes(y = after_stat(density)),
      bins = 30,
      fill = "skyblue",
      colour = "black"
    ) +

    stat_function(
      fun = curve,
      colour = curve_colour,
      linewidth = 1.2,
      args = switch(
        distribution_name,

        "Gamma" = list(
          shape = gamma_fit$estimate["shape"],
          rate = gamma_fit$estimate["rate"]
        ),

        "Exponential" = list(
          rate = exponential_fit$estimate["rate"]
        ),

        "Weibull" = list(
          shape = weibull_fit$estimate["shape"],
          scale = weibull_fit$estimate["scale"]
        )
      )
    ) +

    labs(
      title = distribution_name,
      x = NULL,
      y = "Density"
    ) +

    theme_minimal() +

    theme(
      axis.title.x = element_blank()
    )
}


# Create the three plots
p_gamma <- make_plot(
  dgamma, "Gamma", "red"
)

p_exponential <- make_plot(
  dexp, "Exponential", "blue"
)

p_weibull <- make_plot(
  dweibull, "Weibull", "darkgreen"
)

combined_plot <- (
  p_gamma | p_exponential | p_weibull
) +

  plot_annotation(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budgets",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Comparison of fitted Gamma, Exponential",
      "and Weibull distributions"
    ),
    caption = "Budget (Units of USD 10 Million)"
  ) &

  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 11,
      colour = "black"
    )
  )


# Display the final figure
combined_plot

```

The @fig-budget-qq compare the observed production budgets of Universal Pictures with the fitted Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions. The Gamma and Weibull distributions align more closely with the reference line across most of the budget range, although both deviate for higher-budget films. The Exponential distribution shows greater deviation, suggesting a weaker fit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-budget-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q plots comparing Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions fitted to Universal Pictures' production budgets."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| output: true


n <- length(budget_values)
p <- ppoints(n)
observed <- sort(budget_values)

# Gamma Q-Q plot data
gamma_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qgamma(
    p,
    shape = gamma_fit$estimate["shape"],
    rate = gamma_fit$estimate["rate"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)

# Exponential Q-Q plot data
exponential_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qexp(
    p,
    rate = exponential_fit$estimate["rate"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)

# Weibull Q-Q plot data
weibull_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qweibull(
    p,
    shape = weibull_fit$estimate["shape"],
    scale = weibull_fit$estimate["scale"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)


# Function to create each Q-Q plot
make_qq_plot <- function(qq_data, distribution_name) {

  ggplot(
    qq_data,
    aes(x = theoretical, y = observed)
  ) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    geom_abline(
      intercept = 0,
      slope = 1,
      colour = "red",
      linewidth = 0.7
    ) +
    labs(
      title = distribution_name,
      x = NULL,
      y = "Observed Quantiles"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.title.x = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        hjust = 0.5
      )
    )
}


# Create individual plots
qq_gamma <- make_qq_plot(
  gamma_qq, "Gamma"
)

qq_exponential <- make_qq_plot(
  exponential_qq, "Exponential"
)

qq_weibull <- make_qq_plot(
  weibull_qq, "Weibull"
)


# Combine all three Q-Q plots
combined_qq <- (
  qq_gamma | qq_exponential | qq_weibull
) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Q-Q Plot Comparison of Production Budget Distributions",
    subtitle = "Universal Pictures | Budgets in units of USD 10 million",
    caption = "The red line represents theoretical agreement."
  ) &
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 10
    )
  )

# Display the combined figure
combined_qq
```

## Comparing the AIC for Decision making

The AIC results indicate that the Gamma distribution provides the best relative fit for Universal Pictures’ production budgets, with a score of 1201.090. The Weibull distribution performs almost equally well (1201.542), while the Exponential distribution has a higher AIC (1213.346), indicating a weaker fit. For Meridian Pictures, Gamma is therefore the preferred model for estimating historical budget patterns, although Weibull remains a reasonable alternative.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

aic_table <- data.frame(
  Distribution = c(
    "Gamma",
    "Exponential",
    "Weibull"
  ),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(gamma_fit),
    AIC(exponential_fit),
    AIC(weibull_fit)
  )
)

#creating the table to see clearly

aic_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Fitted Distributions",
    subtitle = "Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Distribution = "Distribution",
    AIC = "AIC Value"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = AIC,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = AIC,
      rows = AIC == min(AIC)
    )
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Lower AIC values indicate a better relative model fit."
  )



```

## Part B

Action films across all studios were analysed to assess downside risk. Numeric variables were checked for missing, zero, negative and infinite values. Zero-budget films were identified because ROI cannot be reliably calculated, while missing and infinite ROI values were excluded. Valid zero and negative ROI values were retained as potentially genuine financial outcomes.

```{r data cleaning for action}


#filtering data
action_data <- movies |>
  filter(
    primary_genre == "Action"
  )

#checking for negative, zero and NA in the filtered data

action_data|>
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      list(
        NA_count = ~sum(is.na(.x)),
        zero_count = ~sum(.x == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        negative_count = ~sum(.x < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )
#looking for negatives, 0 and infinte values in ROI variable

action_data |>
  summarise(
    total_films = n(),
    missing_ROI = sum(is.na(roi)),
    zero_ROI = sum(roi == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    infinite_ROI = sum(!is.finite(roi), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#cleaning the action filtered data

infinite_row <- action_data |> 
  filter(budget == 0 & revenue > 0)

action_data_clean<- action_data |> mutate(
    revenue = ifelse(budget == 0, NA, revenue),
    budget = ifelse(budget==0, NA, budget),
    profit  = ifelse(budget == 0, NA, profit)
  )

```

The 25th percentile of ROI was estimated using non-parametric bootstrapping with 15,000 resamples. This method repeatedly resamples the observed ROI values with replacement, without assuming a specific probability distribution.

The estimated 25th percentile was 0.5764, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4963 to 0.6596. This suggests that the lower-performing quarter of Action films has an ROI threshold of approximately 0.5764, with uncertainty reflected in the confidence interval.

```{r non parametric}
roi_values <- action_data_clean$roi

# Remove missing and infinite values
roi_values <- roi_values[
  !is.na(roi_values) & is.finite(roi_values)
]

# Estimating 25th percentile
q25 <- quantile(roi_values, probs = 0.25)

# Non-parametric bootstrap
set.seed(100)

B <- 15000
n <- length(roi_values)

bootstrap_q25 <- replicate(
  B,
  quantile(
    sample(roi_values, size = n, replace = TRUE),
    probs = 0.25,
    names = FALSE
  )
)

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval
bootstrap_CI <- quantile(
  bootstrap_q25,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
)

# Display results
q25
bootstrap_CI
```

```{r parametric}

# Prepare ROI values
roi_values <- action_data_clean$roi

roi_values <- roi_values[
  !is.na(roi_values) & is.finite(roi_values)
]

# Fit a normal distribution
normal_fit <- fitdistr(roi_values, "normal")

mu <- normal_fit$estimate["mean"]
sigma <- normal_fit$estimate["sd"]

# Estimate the 25th percentile
q25_normal <- qnorm(
  0.25,
  mean = mu,
  sd = sigma
)

# Parametric bootstrap
set.seed(100)

B <- 15000
n <- length(roi_values)

parametric_q25 <- replicate(
  B,
  quantile(
    rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma),
    probs = 0.25,
    names = FALSE
  )
)

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval
parametric_CI <- quantile(
  parametric_q25,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
)

# Display results
q25_normal
parametric_CI

```

# Part C

A normal parametric bootstrap was initially used to compare the results with the non-parametric method. The normal distribution accommodates both positive and negative ROI values, unlike the standard Gamma and Weibull distributions, which require strictly positive values. 

As shown in @tbl-roi-comparison, the non-parametric bootstrap estimates the 25th percentile at 0.5764, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4963–0.6596, while the normal parametric bootstrap estimates it at −0.8080.

The **non-parametric bootstrap** is preferred because it preserves the observed distribution without assuming normality. For Meridian Pictures, this provides a more defensible estimate of lower-end ROI, supporting investment decisions that account for the actual variation in Action-film returns.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-roi-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of 25th Percentile ROI Estimates and 95% Confidence Intervals"
#| echo: false
#| output: true

comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Non-parametric bootstrap",
    "Normal parametric bootstrap"
  ),
  `25th Percentile` = c(
    as.numeric(q25),
    as.numeric(q25_normal)
  ),
  `Lower 95% CI` = c(
    as.numeric(bootstrap_CI[1]),
    as.numeric(parametric_CI[1])
  ),
  `Upper 95% CI` = c(
    as.numeric(bootstrap_CI[2]),
    as.numeric(parametric_CI[2])
  ),
  Suitability = c(
    "Preferred: preserves the observed ROI distribution",
    "Less suitable: assumes normally distributed ROI"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Action Film ROI Estimates",
    subtitle = "25th Percentile and 95% Confidence Intervals"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      `25th Percentile`,
      `Lower 95% CI`,
      `Upper 95% CI`
    ),
    decimals = 4
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Method = "Estimation Method",
    `25th Percentile` = "Estimated Q25",
    `Lower 95% CI` = "Lower Limit",
    `Upper 95% CI` = "Upper Limit",
    Suitability = "Assessment"
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Method,
      rows = Method == "Non-parametric bootstrap"
    )
  )
```

# Part D

Universal Pictures’ production budgets are positively skewed, making the Gamma distribution more suitable than the normal distribution for simulating budget patterns. For Action films, the non-parametric bootstrap estimates the lower-quarter revenue-to-budget ratio at 0.5764, with a confidence interval of approximately 0.467–0.676. 

This suggests that lower-performing Action films generate around 58 cents in revenue per $1 of production budget. This is not a 58% profit or return, as the ratio excludes other costs.

The confidence interval communicates uncertainty around the estimate. Together, these findings help Meridian Pictures simulate realistic budgets and assess potential downside risk when planning future productions.

# Task 4

#Part A: Defining the outcome and justifying the model

A film is defined as a **flop** if it fails to recoup its production budget at the box office, i.e. ROI \< 1. This is created as a binary variable: 1 = flop, 0 = not a flop.




```{r}
movies_clean |>
  summarise(
    total_movies = n(),
    flops = sum(roi < 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    non_flops = sum(roi >= 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    missing_roi = sum(is.na(roi))
  )

movies_model2 <- movies_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(roi)) |>
  mutate(flop = if_else(roi < 1, 1, 0))

genre_focus <- c(
  "Action",
  "Comedy",
  "Drama",
  "Horror",
  "Animation"
)

movies_model2 <- movies_model2 |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% genre_focus)
```

```{r}
#creating modelling dataset
movies_model2<- movies_model2 |>
  mutate(
    flop = if_else(
      roi < 1,
      1L,
      0L,
      missing = NA_integer_
    ),
    log_budget = log(budget)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(flop),
    !is.na(primary_genre),
    !is.na(franchise_status),
    !is.na(log_budget),
    is.finite(log_budget),
    !is.na(cast_size)
  )
```

### Why Logistic Regression?

We use logistic regression to predict whether a film will flop, making this a binary classification problem. Unlike linear regression, which predicts continuous values, logistic regression estimates probabilities between 0 and 1. 

Poisson regression is mainly used for count data. Logistic regression also helps Meridian Pictures understand how factors such as genre, budget and franchise status affect flop probability, supporting more informed greenlight decisions.


### Part B

**Note: Action was selected as the reference genre because its downside risk was examined in the earlier analysis.**

Frequentist and Bayesian logistic regression models were fitted to 2,256 movies. Both produced similar odds ratios and intervals. Animation, Horror, franchise status and cast size were associated with lower flop odds, while Comedy, Drama and log budget showed greater uncertainty. For example, franchise films had approximately 75% lower flop odds than Original films.


```{r}

movies_model2 |>
  mutate(
    primary_genre = relevel(
      factor(primary_genre),
      ref = "Action"
    )
  )

model_freq <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre +
    franchise_status +
    log_budget +
    cast_size,
  data = movies_model2,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
```

```{r}
exp(coef(model_freq))
exp(confint(model_freq))
```

```{r}
results <- broom::tidy(
  model_freq,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  exponentiate = TRUE
) |>
  dplyr::select(
    term,
    estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    Predictor = term,
    `Odds Ratio` = estimate,
    `95% CI Lower` = conf.low,
    `95% CI Upper` = conf.high,
    `P-value` = p.value
  ) 

results |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(`Odds Ratio`, `95% CI Lower`, `95% CI Upper`, `P-value`),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Frequentist Logistic Regression Results",
    subtitle = "Odds Ratios and 95% Confidence Intervals"
  )

```

```{r}

bayesian_model <- stan_glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre +
    franchise_status +
    log_budget +
    cast_size,
  data = movies_model2,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  prior = normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_intercept = normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5, autoscale = FALSE),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 4000,
  seed = 123,
  refresh = 500
)
```

The frequentist and Bayesian intervals were similar. For Animation, the 95% confidence interval was 0.273–0.826, compared with the Bayesian credible interval of 0.275–0.814. For franchise status, the intervals were 0.124–0.444 and 0.127–0.438, respectively. Both intervals lie below 1, indicating lower flop odds. The posterior probability that franchise films have lower flop odds than Original films was approximately 100%, providing strong evidence for this association.

```{r}
posterior_draws <- as.matrix(bayesian_model)

bayes_or <- exp(
  posterior::summarise_draws(
    posterior::as_draws_matrix(bayesian_model)
  )$median
)


tidy(
  bayesian_model,
  effects = "fixed",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
) |>
  mutate(
    `Odds Ratio` = exp(estimate),
    `Lower 95% CrI` = exp(conf.low),
    `Upper 95% CrI` = exp(conf.high)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    term,
    `Odds Ratio`,
    `Lower 95% CrI`,
    `Upper 95% CrI`
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      `Odds Ratio`,
      `Lower 95% CrI`,
      `Upper 95% CrI`
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Predictor"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Bayesian Logistic Regression",
    subtitle = "Odds Ratios and 95% Credible Intervals"
  )
```

The posterior probability that franchise films have lower odds of flopping than Original films is approximately 100%, after controlling for genre, log budget and cast size.



# Appendix: Key Code for Reproducibility

The following condensed code excerpts summarise the main analytical steps used in the report. The complete executable code remains in the project source file.

## A. Data cleaning and derived variables

```r
movies_clean <- movies |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue == 0, NA_real_, as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = revenue / budget,
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )
```

## B. Summary statistics and visualisation

```r
movies_clean |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(budget_m)),
    median_budget = median(budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_roi = median(roi, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(movies_clean, aes(x = budget_m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Production budget ($ millions)", y = "Number of films") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## C. Bootstrap interval for the median-budget difference

```r
set.seed(100)
B <- 5000

boot_diff <- replicate(B, {
  original <- t2 |> filter(franchise_status == "Original") |>
    pull(budget) |> na.omit()
  franchise <- t2 |> filter(franchise_status == "Franchise") |>
    pull(budget) |> na.omit()
  median(sample(franchise, replace = TRUE)) -
    median(sample(original, replace = TRUE))
})

quantile(boot_diff, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
```

## D. Distribution fitting and logistic regression

```r
budget_values <- Universal_budget |>
  filter(!is.na(budget), is.finite(budget), budget > 0) |>
  pull(budget) / 1e7

gamma_fit <- MASS::fitdistr(budget_values, "gamma")
weibull_fit <- MASS::fitdistr(budget_values, "weibull")
exponential_fit <- MASS::fitdistr(budget_values, "exponential")

movies_model2 <- movies_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(roi)) |>
  mutate(flop = as.integer(roi < 1), log_budget = log(budget)) |>
  filter(is.finite(log_budget), !is.na(cast_size),
         !is.na(primary_genre), !is.na(franchise_status))

model_freq <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget + cast_size,
  data = movies_model2,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
```

## E. Bayesian logistic regression

```r
bayesian_model <- rstanarm::stan_glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget + cast_size,
  data = movies_model2,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  prior = normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_intercept = normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = FALSE),
  chains = 4, iter = 4000, seed = 123, refresh = 500
)
```
